title: What is @Conditional and its variants? What is the difference between @SpringBootApplication and @EnableAutoConfiguration? What are the differences between Spring Boot, Spring Framework, and Spring MVC?

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@Conditional` registers beans only when runtime conditions are met. Spring Boot variants: `@ConditionalOnClass` (class on classpath), `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` (user has not defined this bean), `@ConditionalOnProperty` (property set). `@SpringBootApplication` = `@Configuration` + `@EnableAutoConfiguration` + `@ComponentScan`. Spring Framework = core IoC/DI/AOP. Spring MVC = web framework on Servlet API. Spring Boot = opinionated auto-config + embedded server + starters on top of both.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** @Conditional: "Hire a vault guard ONLY IF we have a vault." @SpringBootApplication: the grand opening checklist that registers the branch, auto-sets up equipment, and recruits staff — all in one. Spring Framework = building foundation. Spring MVC = front desk. Spring Boot = turnkey branch manager.

**One line to remember:** @SpringBootApplication = @Configuration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan. @ConditionalOnMissingBean = your @Bean always wins over auto-config.

sections.s2_technical:
**@Conditional variants:** `@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)` — activate when class on classpath (how starters trigger auto-config). `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` — back off when user defines own. `@ConditionalOnProperty(name="feature.enabled", havingValue="true")` — feature flags. `@ConditionalOnWebApplication` / `@ConditionalOnNotWebApplication`.

**Spring Framework vs MVC vs Boot:** Framework = IoC core (manual config, no server). MVC = DispatcherServlet, @Controller (on Servlet API). Boot = auto-config + embedded Tomcat + starters + Actuator + convention over configuration.
sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's interest calculation service needs environment-adaptive features.** In production: Redis cache with real exchange rates. In development: in-memory cache with mock rates. Fraud detection is enabled only via a property flag. The team needs @Conditional to switch beans automatically without if-else logic.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
mvn clean package

# Dev (mock rates, in-memory cache, no fraud check):
java -jar target/interest-calculation-service-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev

# Prod (live rates, Redis cache, fraud check enabled):
java -jar target/interest-calculation-service-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod

# Calculate interest
curl -X POST http://localhost:8091/api/v1/interest/calculate \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"accountId":"SAV2001","principal":500000,"tenureMonths":24}'

# Debug auto-config
java -jar target/interest-calculation-service-1.0.0.jar --debug

mvn test
```
sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1 — Dev profile.** `interest.rate-provider=mock` activates MockRateProvider. No Redis on classpath activates InMemoryCacheService (@ConditionalOnMissingBean). `interest.fraud-check-enabled=false` means FraudCheckService bean is NOT created.

**Step 2 — Prod profile.** `interest.rate-provider=live` activates LiveRateProvider. Redis classes on classpath activates RedisCacheService. `interest.fraud-check-enabled=true` creates FraudCheckService.

**Step 3 — Request.** InterestService receives `Optional<FraudCheckService>`. In dev: Optional.empty() — fraud check skipped. In prod: Optional with real service — fraud check runs.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Conditional annotation is the foundation of Spring Boot's auto-configuration. ConditionalOnClass activates beans when a class is on the classpath — this is how adding a starter dependency triggers configuration. ConditionalOnMissingBean backs off when you define your own bean — your custom configuration always wins. ConditionalOnProperty enables feature flags: a bean is created only when a specific property is set to a specific value.

SpringBootApplication combines three annotations: Configuration marks the class as a bean source, EnableAutoConfiguration triggers classpath-based auto-configuration, and ComponentScan discovers annotated components. Spring Framework is the core IoC container with manual configuration. Spring MVC is the web framework on the Servlet API. Spring Boot adds auto-configuration, embedded server, starters, and Actuator.

In my banking interest calculation service, ConditionalOnProperty switches between LiveRateProvider in production and MockRateProvider in development — no if-else logic in code. ConditionalOnClass activates RedisCacheService when Redis is on the classpath, and ConditionalOnMissingBean provides InMemoryCacheService as a fallback in development. FraudCheckService is created only when a feature flag property is true, and InterestService injects it as Optional so it works correctly regardless of whether the bean exists. Zero code changes between environments — only profile properties change.
